explanation: Double-quoted strings are parsed for variables and escape sequences like \n, while single-quoted strings treat them literally, so they are not processed identically.
The null coalescing operator (??) evaluates its left operand like isset(), so undefined variables produce no error or warning.
echo can take multiple comma-separated arguments and outputs them in order, so it prints 'ab'.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions.
The elvis operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, and its right operand only when the left operand is falsy.
In PHP 8, the concatenation operator '.' was moved to a lower precedence than '+' and '-', so arithmetic is evaluated before concatenation.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so the expression evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512.
In PHP 8, the + operator has higher precedence than ., so it evaluates as 'sum: ' . (2 + 3).
Strict comparison (===) requires arrays to have the same key/value pairs in the same order with identical types.
The == operator is a loose comparison, and 0 == false actually returns true; strict comparison would use ===.
Since PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number converts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 is false (it was true in PHP 7).
In loose comparison, null == 0, null == "", and null == false all evaluate to true because null is cast to each type for comparison.
Casting a string to int takes the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer, so the addition yields 10.
Casting false to string yields an empty string "", while true becomes "1".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not identical (===) to 0.3.
strrev() operates on bytes, so multi-byte UTF-8 characters become garbled instead of properly reversed.
str_contains() returns true because 'world' exists in 'Hello world'.
str_pad() supports padding on the right (default), left, or both sides via the optional pad_type argument (STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default trim() strips whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen() counts bytes, and 'é' occupies 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 'héllo' is 6 bytes.
A negative start value of -3 counts from the end of the string, returning the last 3 characters.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; PHP strings are immutable and are not modified in place.
Heredoc syntax (<<<EOT) parses variables inside the string, while nowdoc syntax (<<<'EOT') treats the content literally without interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array with numeric keys, so it does not preserve key-value associations (asort() does).
PHP automatically casts array keys that are valid decimal integers (like '5') to the integer type.
in_array() uses loose comparison by default; strict (===) comparison is only used when the third $strict parameter is set to true.
When called without a callback, array_filter() keeps only elements that evaluate to true (truthy), removing values like false, 0, '', null, '0', and empty arrays.
By default, array_slice() reindexes numeric keys; you must pass true as the fourth parameter ($preserve_keys) to keep the original keys.
array_slice extracts 2 elements starting at offset 1, returning elements 20 and 30.
The union operator keeps the left array's value for the duplicate key 'a' and adds the new key 'b', yielding 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator, which previously only worked with integer keys.
Named arguments can be combined with argument unpacking; a spread array with string keys even produces named arguments, and you can mix spread and explicit named arguments in one call.
Anonymous functions in PHP do not inherit outer scope variables unless imported explicitly via the use clause.
func_num_args() returns the actual number of arguments passed to the function, regardless of the declared parameters, so f(1, 2, 3) yields 3.
An arrow function's body must be a single expression; multiple statements in curly braces are only allowed in the longer `function` syntax.
Arrow functions capture outer variables by value (automatically, by-value copy at definition time), unlike anonymous functions which use explicit & in use().
A closure declared with the static keyword cannot automatically bind $this, so it does not capture the current object context.
The variable is captured by value (copied) when the closure is created, so changing $x afterwards doesn't affect it.
In weak typing mode, PHP coerces the numeric string "5" to the int 5, so it is accepted for an int parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers directly in constructor parameters.
The 'final' keyword marks a method so that child classes cannot override it.
The final keyword prevents a method from being overridden by child classes.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that declares them; subclasses must use protected or public visibility to inherit access.
Anonymous classes are named class@anonymous followed by a NUL byte and the file path and line number, so the part before the NUL byte is class@anonymous.
Private methods are not inherited, so a child class can freely declare a same-named method with any visibility without conflicting with the parent's signature.
__get() is called for inaccessible properties, which includes both non-existent properties and existing properties that are not accessible (e.g., private or protected).
Reassigning a readonly property throws an Error (Cannot modify readonly property), not an Exception, because it is a logic error.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which are inherited by classes implementing the interface.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a class or implements an interface.
Since PHP 5.3 (and fully supported with signatures in later versions), interfaces may declare static methods that implementing classes must define.
instanceof returns true not only for class inheritance but also when the object implements the given interface.
In PHP, interface methods only declare a signature and cannot contain any implementation body, unlike trait methods which provide default behavior.
Abstract methods in PHP may be declared public or protected, so protected visibility is allowed.
Foo::cases() returns an array of all enum cases, and this enum defines three cases: A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which are then available to classes that use the trait.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError inherits from Error, not Exception, so a catch (Exception $e) block will not catch it.
The @ operator only suppresses errors and warnings; exceptions always propagate and cannot be suppressed.
In PHP 7+, intdiv(5, 0) throws a DivisionByZeroError, which is a subclass of ArithmeticError.
The finally block always executes, whether or not the exception was caught, and even runs if the exception propagates uncaught.
An exception thrown inside a finally block overrides (discards) any return value or pending exception from the try/catch blocks.
Any object, including an Exception instance, is always truthy when cast to bool.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed when script execution stops, including when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only creates an alias; the class file is loaded by the autoloader only when the class is actually referenced at runtime.
In PHP, `use function` imports a function into the current namespace, while `use const` imports a constant.
PSR-4 replaces the App\ prefix with src/, so the remaining namespace path maps to Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php registers its class loader with spl_autoload_register(), not __autoload().
The __NAMESPACE__ magic constant holds the name of the current namespace, or an empty string at global scope.
An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace, not the global root; only a name with a leading `\` refers to the global namespace.
Under PSR-4, the namespace prefix App\ is replaced by the base directory src/, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.

Namespace import (use) statements may only appear at the top level of a file or namespace block — placing one inside a function is a parse error, and even if allowed it would apply to the whole file, not just that function.
In PHP, arrays use copy-on-value semantics: assigning one variable's array to another creates a copy unless a reference (&) is explicitly used.
PHP arrays are copied by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.

PHP functions have their own local scope, so user-defined global variables can only be accessed inside a function via the global keyword, the $GLOBALS superglobal array, or by passing them as parameters.
Unsetting $GLOBALS['x'] removes the global variable itself from the global scope, affecting all code, not just the current function.
The parameter is passed by reference, so $x++ modifies $n directly.
When foreach iterates by value, it operates on a copy of the array, so modifications made inside the loop do not affect the iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared by all instances, so changes are visible to every object.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers (true becomes 1, false becomes 0), so they are stored as ints, not as bool.
Since PHP 7.0, a generator may return a final value via return, retrievable after the generator finishes using $gen->getReturn().
Generators are forward-only iterators; once exhausted, calling rewind() throws an Exception because iteration cannot be restarted.
yield from delegates iteration to another generator, Traversable, or array, effectively running it and forwarding its yielded values.
Calling a generator function returns a Generator object, so get_class returns 'Generator'.
iterator_to_array by default preserves keys (0, 1, 2), so the array has three elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO (last-in-first-out) stack; SplQueue is the class that implements FIFO behavior.
ArrayIterator wraps an array or object and lets you traverse it using the Iterator interface methods like rewind(), current(), key(), next(), and valid().
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so foreach can traverse it.
password_hash() generates a cryptographically secure salt itself, and the salt option is deprecated/ignored.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT in PHP 8 is bcrypt (password_hash with a salt), not md5.
password_hash generates a salted hash whose salt is embedded in the returned string, so password_verify('secret', ...) correctly returns true.
strip_tags() only removes HTML and PHP tags; SQL injection should be prevented with prepared statements or proper escaping functions.
Calling session_regenerate_id() after login generates a new session ID, preventing attackers from fixing a known session ID on a victim.
The php_sapi_name() function returns the name of the interface between PHP and the web server, such as 'cli'.
session_destroy() removes server-side session data, but the client-side session cookie must be deleted separately, e.g. with setcookie().
$_SESSION is only populated after session_start() (or session.auto_start enabled) loads the session data.
array_find() was added in PHP 8.4, returning the first element of an array that satisfies a callback.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get and set logic to be defined directly in property declarations.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g., public private(set)) was introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing read and write visibility to differ.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which warns when a function's return value is discarded, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5 via the Pipe Operator RFC, allowing value passing through a chain of callable functions.
The clone-with syntax for initializing readonly properties was introduced in PHP 8.3.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were introduced in PHP 8.5.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was accepted for PHP 8.5.
The clamp_v2 RFC was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.5, released in November 2025.
The Context Managers RFC had not been adopted into PHP as of late 2025; it was still only a proposal and no PHP release includes it.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC was voted down and officially declined in early 2026.
No RFC has been accepted to make PHP thread-safe (ZTS) by default; ZTS remains an optional build configuration.
As of PHP 8.5, generics/parameterized types have still not been implemented in the language.
PHP 8.5 was released in November 2025, while PHP 8.6's GA is scheduled for November 19, 2026, so as of 2026-11-07 PHP 8.5 is the latest stable version.
The PHP 6 project was abandoned and PHP 5.6 was followed directly by PHP 7.0 in 2015.
The RFC introducing the #[\Deprecated] attribute was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4.
In clean/onion architecture, dependencies point inward so inner layers (domain/core) have no knowledge of outer layers (infrastructure, UI).
In clean/hexagonal architecture, domain entities stay framework-agnostic and depend only on plain PHP and its standard library.
Controllers and templates belong to the presentation/application layer; the business-logic layer is the domain code containing the use cases themselves, not the code that merely calls them.
In onion architecture, the innermost core layer is the domain model (entities and business rules), with all other layers wrapping around it.
Tools like deptrac statically analyze code against defined layer rules and fail the build when a forbidden dependency is detected.

An interactor should depend only on domain concepts (DTOs, entities, value objects), not on HTTP requests or an EntityManager, which are delivery/infrastructure concerns that must stay outside the use case layer.
A Repository encapsulates a collection of aggregates/entities and hides the underlying storage mechanism behind an interface.
Database access is an infrastructure detail in the outer layer; the domain and use cases depend only on abstractions (interfaces), so the implementation can be swapped without changing them.
An aggregate is a domain-driven design concept: a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency boundary, which may span multiple tables.
A Value Object is defined by being immutable and compared by the values of its fields rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single external entry point through which all modifications to an aggregate must pass.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined only for aggregate roots, since other entities within an aggregate are accessed and persisted through their root.
In Domain-Driven Design, ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary used consistently by developers and domain experts, and it is reflected in the model.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while the same terms outside may refer to different models.
In DDD, the anemic model is considered an anti-pattern; the recommended style is a rich domain model where behavior lives with the data.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a self-contained model, so the same real-world concept is represented by separate classes in different contexts.
Symfony services are instantiated only when they are first requested, unless marked as synthetic or eager via public/shared configurations like the 'lazy' option being false by design.
The Symfony console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony autowiring automatically registers and injects services, so manual declaration of every service in services.yaml is not required.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes and caches them, so they are only recompiled when the template source changes.
In the dev environment Symfony tracks config files, classes, and other resources and rebuilds the DI container only when one of them changes, otherwise it reuses the cached container.
Symfony uses the APP_ENV environment variable to select the active environment, such as dev or prod.
Symfony's controller resolver invokes the method via PHP Reflection (ReflectionMethod), which can call private/protected methods, so routing works with them.
Subscribers are just listeners registered via getSubscribedEvents(); they have no inherent priority and can even define their own priority per event.
Symfony 6.0 removed the deprecated Guard authenticator system, making AuthenticatorInterface-based security the standard approach.
The #[IsGranted] attribute checks a security role/permission on a controller action and throws a 403 AccessDeniedException if the check fails.
Symfony voters are the mechanism used with isGranted()/denyAccessUnlessGranted() to decide whether access to a specific object (like a Post) is allowed for a given attribute such as 'EDIT'.
Since Symfony 6.3/7.0, validation constraints must use PHP attributes and legacy doctrine/annotations support has been removed.
Symfony forms have CSRF protection enabled by default and automatically validate the token when the form is submitted.
Symfony validation always runs on the server when the form is submitted, regardless of client-side HTML5 validation results.
Symfony MakerBundle's `make:form` command generates a new form class (FormType).
Symfony never stores the password in the session; after authentication it only keeps the authenticated token/user, so the password is not stored at all.
In modern Symfony applications, bundle configuration files like framework.yaml, twig.yaml, and doctrine.yaml are stored in the config/packages directory, typically one file per bundle or topic.
In Symfony, .env holds committed defaults while .env.local stores real secrets and is excluded via .gitignore.
The Symfony console command 'debug:container' lists registered services and their aliases (known as container:debug in older Symfony versions).
The Symfony service container is compiled and frozen before runtime, so calling setParameter() from a controller throws a LogicException ('Impossible to call set() on a frozen ParameterBag').
By default Symfony services are private (public: false), so they can only be injected via autowiring or the container cannot be used to fetch them directly.
Bundles work with their default settings; configuration files in config/packages are optional and only needed to override defaults.
In Symfony's services.yaml, environment variables are referenced with the %env(VAR)% syntax.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable to enable or disable debug mode, which controls the profiler and Twig debugging.
Symfony Messenger allows a message to be handled by multiple handlers; all matching handlers receive it.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process instead of sending it to a queue for a worker.
The Symfony command `php bin/console messenger:consume` starts the worker that processes messages from the Messenger transports.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy option is defined under each individual transport in the framework.messenger.transports configuration.
By default, Symfony Messenger uses the PhpSerializer (PHP's serialize function); JSON encoding is opt-in via the Serializer component.
The Symfony Scheduler component produces scheduled messages and dispatches them via Messenger transports to trigger handlers at the scheduled times.
The doctrine Messenger transport stores queued messages in database tables via Doctrine (e.g., using messenger_messages table).
Symfony Messenger buses are a middleware stack, so custom middleware can be injected into the stack (before or after the built-in middleware like validation, sending, or handling).
Symfony follows a scheduled release policy with major versions every two years and minor versions every six months, in May and November.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.3 or higher.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations; you must use PHP attributes, XML, YAML, or PHP configuration instead.
AssetMapper (introduced in Symfony 6.3/7.0) lets you manage CSS/JS via importmap.php without needing Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (long-term support) release with extended bug fixes and security support until 2027.
Major Symfony releases remove all features that were deprecated in the previous major branch.
Each Symfony major release includes an UPGRADE guide (e.g., UPGRADE-6.0.md) documenting the changes and migration steps.
The Symfony AssetMapper component manages JavaScript/CSS assets and importmaps natively, without requiring Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 would be released late November 2026, so on 2026-11-07 it has not yet been released.
Symfony follows a six-month release cycle with minor versions in May and November, so Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for November 2026, two releases after the 8.0 launch in November 2025.
Symfony follows a scheme where the next minor release after 8.1 is 8.2.
In Symfony's SemVer scheme, releases like 8.2 are minor releases that are backward-compatible and do not require rewriting applications.
Within a major version branch (e.g., 8.1 to 8.2), PHP maintains backward compatibility, so code should continue to work without modification.
Symfony follows a pattern where the last minor release of a major branch is x.4 (released alongside the next major), so 8.4 is the final 8.x release before 9.0.
Symfony only raises its minimum PHP version at major releases (Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.4), so minor releases like 8.2 keep the same PHP requirement rather than jumping to 8.5.
Symfony's policy is that deprecations introduced in a major branch (8.x) may only be removed in the next major version (9.0).
Twig is a sandboxed template engine that only allows its own syntax, filters, and registered functions/macros, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig's default environment enables auto-escaping with the 'html' strategy, so printed variables are escaped automatically unless disabled.
The Twig |e filter escapes a string for safe output in HTML (and other strategies) contexts.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to the given locale (e.g. {{ 1000|format_number(locale='fr') }}).
The |raw filter marks a value as safe, so Twig's auto-escaping is not applied to it.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs the value of an expression, while {% %} executes control-flow tags like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside a template using the {% set %} tag.
The dump() Twig function outputs the debug information of a variable when the debug mode is enabled.
Bootstrap provides prebuilt CSS and JavaScript UI components, whereas SPA frameworks (like Angular, React, or Vue) manage application structure and state.
The .container class provides a responsive fixed-width container whose max-width changes at each breakpoint.
The Bootstrap grid is divided into 12 columns, not 16.
Bootstrap 5 defines the infixes sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl for its named breakpoints (with no infix needed for extra-small).
In Bootstrap-style utility classes, the numeric suffix is a multiplier of the $spacer variable (e.g., .mt-3 equals 3 × $spacer).
In Bootstrap 5, interactive components like dropdowns are enabled with the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown").
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency, so all components work with plain vanilla JavaScript.
In Bootstrap 5.3 dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the html element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not create tables automatically at runtime; schema creation must be done explicitly via the SchemaTool or migrations.
EntityManager::persist() tells Doctrine to manage a new entity, but the INSERT SQL is deferred until flush() is called.
In Doctrine ORM 3 the merge() method was removed from the EntityManager, and even in ORM 2 it never made the passed object itself managed but returned a managed copy.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) operates on entities, their fields, and relationships rather than database tables and columns.
In Doctrine, find() returns null when no entity matches the given identifier.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically flush; you must call flush() explicitly in your code to persist changes.
Once an entity is managed, Doctrine's Unit of Work automatically detects changes at flush(), so persist() is only needed for new entities.
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the DELETE SQL is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC in PostgreSQL allows readers and writers to work concurrently without blocking each other.
The EXPLAIN statement shows the query execution plan without actually running the query.

SERIAL is legacy shorthand that creates a sequence-backed default nextval column, while GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard identity column with stricter rules (e.g., manual inserts are blocked unless OVERRIDING is used).
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct, so a UNIQUE column can contain multiple rows with NULL by default (unlike SQL Server).
PostgreSQL's string_agg() aggregate function concatenates strings from multiple rows using a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table files but does not shrink them; only VACUUM FULL returns space to the operating system.
In SQL window functions, the PARTITION BY clause divides rows into groups (partitions) over which the function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; each new read can see committed changes from other transactions, so non-repeatable reads can still occur (REPEATABLE READ is the level that prevents them).
PostgreSQL executes each standalone statement in its own implicit transaction and commits it immediately unless an explicit transaction is started.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes to the database.
Indexes help locate matching rows quickly, so UPDATE and DELETE statements with WHERE conditions on indexed columns also benefit.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to create points within a transaction that can be rolled back to with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT.
EXPLAIN only shows the plan without executing; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real timing and row counts.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that provides vector data types and similarity-search indexes (IVFFlat, HNSW) for embeddings.
A partial index only contains entries for rows that satisfy its WHERE clause, making it smaller and faster for matching queries.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) using predicate locks to detect serialization conflicts, not by locking the rows a transaction reads.
HTTP 201 is the 'Created' status, indicating the request resulted in a new resource being created.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates the request succeeded and the response has no body.
Per RFC 7231 (and 9110), DELETE is defined as idempotent, so repeating it on the same resource leaves the same end state (the resource remains deleted/non-existent).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server, not the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access the resource.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests is specifically returned when a client has sent too many requests within a given time, i.e., exceeded a rate limit.
It's the opposite: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header describes the MIME type of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas RFC 9110 requires PUT to be idempotent.
Plain == is vulnerable to timing attacks and loose-comparison quirks; you should use password_verify() or hash_equals() instead.
CSRF protection works by having the server issue a token tied to the session and validate it on state-changing requests like POST.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP header is used to deliver the CSP policy to browsers.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that grants delegated access via tokens; it does not define or guarantee user authentication (that's OpenID Connect's role).
XSS must be prevented by escaping output in the appropriate context when rendering (e.g., htmlspecialchars), not merely by validating input before storing it.
The authorization server redirects to the redirect_uri with a 'code' (authorization code) parameter, which the client exchanges for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens, which are short-lived, without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
The salt does not need to be kept secret; it is stored alongside the hash and used during verification, and its security value comes from uniqueness, not secrecy.
PHPUnit only discovers and runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase.
setUp() runs before each individual test method; the method that runs once before all tests is setUpBeforeClass().
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, so the test runs once for each data set it returns.
PHPUnit's expectException() method declares that the tested code is expected to throw an exception of the given class.
It's the reverse: stubs return canned data, while mocks verify which methods were called.
PHPUnit 10 introduced metadata attributes such as #[DataProvider], deprecating the @dataProvider annotation.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, allowing a test to receive the output of a producer test.
PHPUnit 7.2+ runs tests in random order when passed --order-by=random (optionally combined with --random-order-seed for reproducibility).
